nt.bh.title: Black holes
nt.bh.summary: Fly to a real black hole, watch it bend the sky and slow time, then fall in.
nt.bh.intro.title: What is a black hole?
nt.bh.intro.text: A place where so much mass is packed into so small a space that nothing escapes its gravity, not even light. Its boundary is the event horizon. The marked point, about 1,900 light-years away in the constellation Aquila, is Gaia BH3, a black hole left behind by a single massive star. We are flying there.
nt.bh.bh3.title: Gaia BH3
nt.bh.bh3.text: {bh3_mass} times the mass of the Sun, yet its event horizon has a radius of only about {bh3_rs} km. It gives off no light: Gaia found it from the wobble of the old giant star that circles it every 11.6 years. The sky behind it is the real sky mapped by Gaia, and as we come closer its gravity bends that starlight.
nt.bh.ring.title: Bent light: the Einstein ring
nt.bh.ring.text: Gravity bends the path of light. Stars right behind the hole are smeared into a bright circle, the Einstein ring, and some stars appear twice, once on each side. The black disc in the middle is the shadow: light that would have come from there fell in. We circle the hole so you can watch the sky slide around it.
nt.bh.time.title: Time runs slower
nt.bh.time.text: Watch the two clocks on the panel. Hovering at 6 Schwarzschild radii, each second of yours lasts {bh3_slow6} seconds for someone far away. You would notice nothing: your heart and your watch tick as usual. Gravity slows time itself, and the closer you get, the bigger the gap.
nt.bh.tides.title: Spaghettification
nt.bh.tides.text: At 3 Schwarzschild radii, gravity pulls on your feet far harder than on your head. Across a 2-metre body the difference is {bh3_tid3} g, a stretch that would tear any person or spacecraft apart. Astronomers really call this spaghettification. One second of yours now lasts {bh3_slow3} seconds far away.
nt.bh.photon.title: The photon sphere
nt.bh.photon.text: At 1.5 Schwarzschild radii light itself can travel in a circle around the hole. The map stops you here: closer in, no rocket could hold you in place. The stretch has reached {bh3_tid15} g. Around a giant like Sgr A* the same place is gentle, only {sgr_tid15} g, because its horizon is far wider.
nt.bh.sgra.title: Sgr A*, the giant at the centre of our Galaxy
nt.bh.sgra.text: Sgr A* weighs {sgr_mass} Suns, measured from the orbits of the stars around it, and its event horizon has a radius of about {sgr_rs} km. The glowing ring is an illustrative disk of hot gas spiralling in, brighter on the side that moves towards us. The real Sgr A* feeds through a hot, thick flow that the Event Horizon Telescope sees in radio.
nt.bh.fall.title: Falling in
nt.bh.fall.text: Imagine falling on, past the horizon. For a hole this big you would feel nothing special as you cross it. A distant watcher would never see you cross: your image would slow down, redden and fade. What happens inside can never be seen from outside. Einstein's theory predicts a singularity, where the theory itself breaks down. This fade to black is an illustration, not a simulation.
nt.bh.m87.title: M87*, the first picture of a black hole
nt.bh.m87.text: {m87_mass} Suns, 55 million light-years away in the galaxy M87. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, radio dishes across the Earth working as one, showed a glowing ring of gas around its dark shadow, 42 micro-arcseconds across. Its event horizon is wider than the whole distance Voyager 1 has travelled since 1977.
nt.bh.gw.title: When black holes collide
nt.bh.gw.text: On 14 September 2015 the LIGO detectors felt space itself shake: two black holes of about 35 and 30 Suns, some 430 Mpc away, merged into one of about 62. The missing mass left as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second. Each soft cloud here is the region where one of 282 measured mergers happened.
nt.mw.title: The Milky Way
nt.mw.summary: Our home galaxy: nearby stars, star nurseries, dust, spiral arms, the centre and our neighbours.
nt.mw.sun.title: Our star
nt.mw.sun.text: The Sun is one of more than 100 billion stars in the Milky Way. With all its planets it circles the centre of the Galaxy at about 247 km/s, one lap in roughly 200 to 230 million years. Since it formed, it has gone around only some twenty times.
nt.mw.near.title: Gaia's bubble
nt.mw.near.text: Every point here is a real star measured by the Gaia satellite, out to 1 kpc from the Sun. Each one has its measured colour: blue-white stars are hot, orange-red ones are cool. This whole bubble is only a small piece of the Galaxy's disc.
nt.mw.orion.title: A star nursery: the Orion Nebula
nt.mw.orion.text: The closest large star-forming region, 433 pc away, visible to the naked eye below the belt of Orion. Inside the glowing gas, dense clumps collapse into new stars; four massive young stars, the Trapezium, light it up. Clouds like this can hold 1,000 to 10 million times the mass of the Sun.
nt.mw.pleiades.title: Born together: the Pleiades
nt.mw.pleiades.text: Stars are rarely born alone. The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, are more than a thousand stars that formed together about 120 million years ago, 135 pc from us. In the Gaia data they stand out as a tight group at the same distance, moving the same way.
nt.mw.dust.title: Dark clouds of dust
nt.mw.dust.text: Between the stars drift clouds of fine dust. This is a real 3D map of them (Edenhofer et al. 2024), out to 1.25 kpc from the Sun. Seen from inside the disc, such clouds are the dark lanes that split the band of the Milky Way in the night sky, and they hide distant stars from visible light.
nt.mw.arms.title: The spiral arms
nt.mw.arms.text: From far above, the Milky Way is a barred spiral more than 100,000 light-years across. Radio telescopes measured the distances of about 200 star-forming regions through the dust; their positions suggest four main spiral arms. This picture is a model built from those measurements: nobody has a photograph of our Galaxy from outside.
nt.mw.centre.title: The Galactic Centre
nt.mw.centre.text: 8.3 kpc (27,000 light-years) from the Sun, behind thick dust in Sagittarius, lies the centre. The star S2 circles an invisible mass there once every 16 years, and its orbit weighs that mass at {sgr_mass} Suns: the black hole Sgr A*.
nt.mw.orbits.title: Stars on the move
nt.mw.orbits.text: Nothing here stands still. The clock now runs 30 million years ahead: each star follows its own orbit around the Galactic Centre, computed from its Gaia velocity, and the neighbourhood slowly spreads apart. Positions are shown relative to the Sun.
nt.mw.clouds.title: Satellite galaxies: the Magellanic Clouds
nt.mw.clouds.text: Small galaxies orbit ours. The Large Magellanic Cloud is 49.59 kpc away, a distance measured to about 1 % with eclipsing binary stars; the Small Magellanic Cloud is at about 64 kpc. From the southern sky both are visible to the naked eye.
nt.mw.m31.title: Andromeda, our big neighbour
nt.mw.m31.text: The Andromeda Galaxy, 783 kpc away, is the other giant of the Local Group. Its light set out about 2.6 million years ago. Andromeda and the Milky Way are often said to be on a collision course, but a 2024 study found a probability of close to 50 % that they do not merge in the next 10 billion years.
nt.life.title: Life of a star
nt.life.summary: From a cloud of gas to a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole.
nt.life.cloud.title: Born in a cloud
nt.life.cloud.text: Stars are born in cold clouds of gas and dust like the Orion Nebula. Gravity pulls dense clumps together until their cores are hot enough to fuse hydrogen into helium. That fusion releases the energy that makes a star shine.
nt.life.cluster.title: A family of stars
nt.life.cluster.text: One collapsing cloud makes many stars at once. The Pleiades were born together about 120 million years ago: the same age, the same starting chemistry, only different masses. Mass decides almost everything that follows. Massive stars burn fast and may live only a few million years.
nt.life.sun.title: A long, quiet middle age
nt.life.sun.text: A star like the Sun spends most of its life quietly fusing hydrogen in its core. Every second the Sun turns about 4.26 million tonnes of its mass into energy. It is about 4.6 billion years old, a little less than halfway through its life.
nt.life.giant.title: Swelling into a giant
nt.life.giant.text: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, a star swells. In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant. Heavier stars swell even more: Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion, is a red supergiant.
nt.life.pn.title: A planetary nebula
nt.life.pn.text: A Sun-like star then gently blows off its outer layers, which glow for a while as a planetary nebula. The Helix Nebula, about 200 pc away, is one. The name is old and misleading: William Herschel thought such nebulae looked like the disc of the planet Uranus.
nt.life.wd.title: A white dwarf
nt.life.wd.text: What remains is the bare, hot core: a white dwarf. Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, has one: Sirius B, 98 % of the Sun's mass in a ball about 12,000 km across, smaller than the Earth. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh about 5 tonnes. The Sun will end this way.
nt.life.sn.title: A supernova
nt.life.sn.text: A star of about 8 Suns or more ends violently: its core collapses and the rest is blasted into space. In 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded such a new star in Taurus. Its remnant is the Crab Nebula, about 6,500 light-years away, still flying apart at more than 1,300 km/s.
nt.life.pulsar.title: A neutron star
nt.life.pulsar.text: At the Crab's heart is the collapsed core: a neutron star about 20 km across that holds more mass than the Sun. It spins 30 times every second and sweeps beams of radio waves past the Earth like a lighthouse, so we see it as a pulsar. A sugar cube of its matter would weigh about a trillion kilograms.
nt.life.bh.title: A black hole
nt.life.bh.text: If the collapsing core is heavier than about 3 Suns, nothing can stop it: it becomes a black hole. Gaia BH3, {bh3_mass} Suns, is the heaviest black hole of stellar origin known in our Galaxy. Its companion star is very poor in metals, a clue that such heavy black holes come from metal-poor stars.
nt.uni.title: The universe
nt.uni.summary: From our group of galaxies to the cosmic web, quasars and the oldest light.
nt.uni.lg.title: The Local Group
nt.uni.lg.text: Zoom out from the Milky Way and you meet our family of galaxies, the Local Group, about 3 Mpc across. Two big spirals dominate it, the Milky Way and Andromeda, and more than 100 smaller galaxies are known around them.
nt.uni.virgo.title: The Virgo Cluster
nt.uni.virgo.text: About 16.5 Mpc (54 million light-years) away lies a crowded cluster of galaxies, home of the giant galaxy M87 and its black hole. It was long thought to be the centre of our “Local Supercluster”. In fact it is only one small part of something much bigger.
nt.uni.laniakea.title: Laniakea, our supercluster
nt.uni.laniakea.text: Galaxies do not only drift apart with the expansion: they also stream towards dense regions. These lines trace that flow (Cosmicflows-4). All galaxies in our basin, Laniakea, about 500 million light-years across with about 100,000 large galaxies, flow towards the Great Attractor, about 100 Mpc away. The Milky Way sits on the outskirts.
nt.uni.web.title: The cosmic web
nt.uni.web.text: Further out, galaxies form a web: long filaments, flat walls and huge empty voids. This thin slice comes from DESI, which measured 15,140,002 galaxies and quasars in its first data release. Light from the far side of its map left about 11 billion years ago: the deeper you look, the younger the universe you see.
nt.uni.quasars.title: Quasars
nt.uni.quasars.text: The pale cyan points are quasars, the brilliant cores of distant galaxies, powered by gas falling into supermassive black holes. DESI has 1,583,866 of them. Beyond redshift 2 every object here is a quasar; the farthest reach redshift 6.8, light that left them about 13 billion years ago.
nt.uni.cmb.title: The oldest light
nt.uni.cmb.text: This is as far as light can reach us from: the cosmic microwave background. When the universe was about 380,000 years old, its hot fog cleared and this light set out. The gas that sent it is now about 13.9 Gpc (45 billion light-years) away. Today it is a glow at 2.7255 K, with ripples of one part in 100,000: the seeds of all galaxies.
nt.uni.expansion.title: Stretched light
nt.uni.expansion.text: Why is that light so cold? Space has been stretching while the light travelled, and the light waves stretched with it: this is redshift. At redshift z = 1 the universe was half its present size. It is also why light that travelled for 13 billion years comes from a place that is now 8.74 Gpc away.
nt.sol.title: The Solar System
nt.sol.summary: The Sun, the planets, asteroids and comets, the Moon, Mars and Voyager 1.
nt.sol.sun.title: The Sun
nt.sol.sun.text: The Sun holds 99.8 % of all the mass in the Solar System. Its radius is 695,700 km, 109 times the Earth's, and its light needs 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach us.
nt.sol.planets.title: Eight planets
nt.sol.planets.text: Seen from above, eight planets circle the Sun in nearly one plane: four rocky ones close in, then four giants. Neptune, the outermost, is 30.2 au out; sunlight needs about 4.2 hours to get there. Jupiter alone has about 2.5 times the mass of all the other planets put together.
nt.sol.belt.title: Asteroids and trojans
nt.sol.belt.text: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt: 1,396,520 catalogued main-belt asteroids (sand), out of 1,580,494 asteroids known in all. Jupiter's trojans (green) share its orbit. For all their numbers, together they have less mass than our Moon.
nt.sol.comet.title: Halley's comet
nt.sol.comet.text: Comets are dirty snowballs a few kilometres across. Near the Sun their ice turns to gas and they grow a glowing coma and tails that always point away from the Sun. Halley's comet comes back every 75 to 76 years. In late 2026 it is near its farthest point, 35 au out; it returns on 14 August 2061.
nt.sol.moon.title: The Moon: crater Tycho
nt.sol.moon.text: Tycho, 85 km wide, is named after the astronomer Tycho Brahe. The Moon has almost no air, so its ground swings from about 117 °C by day to −178 °C at night. Twelve people have walked on it. The clock is set to 24 November 2026, when the Sun is up over Tycho.
nt.sol.mars.title: Mars: Gale crater
nt.sol.mars.text: Gale crater, 154 km wide, lies near the Martian equator; NASA's Curiosity rover landed inside it. The air here is thin, about 6 millibars and 95 % carbon dioxide, yet orbiters and rovers have found dried-up river valleys, deltas and old lakebeds: Mars once had liquid water.
nt.sol.voyager.title: Voyager 1
nt.sol.voyager.text: Launched on 5 September 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant object people have made: about 172 au from the Sun in November 2026, moving at about 17 km/s. In 2012, at 121.6 au, it left the bubble of the solar wind. NASA expects it to reach one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.
nt.sol.proxima.title: The nearest star
nt.sol.proxima.text: After the Sun, the nearest star is Proxima Centauri, a small red dwarf 4.24 light-years away. Even at Voyager 1's speed the trip would take about 75,000 years. The light you see from it tonight left 4.24 years ago.
